tagline.text: A 1916 neoclassical customs house above the river wharf, now home to a maritime history museum

location.label: Location
location.text: Corner of Muelle Loney Street and Aduana Street, Iloilo City Proper

children.text: This neoclassical customs house on Muelle Loney Street, at the mouth of the Iloilo River, was completed in 1916. Customs and immigration offices still work here, and the ground floor holds a maritime history museum with free admission.

The Iloilo Customs House, also known by its Spanish name Aduana, stands on the bank of the Iloilo River in Iloilo City Proper, the city's downtown. It sits at the corner of Muelle Loney Street and Aduana Street, and its defining feature is the central tower rising from the middle of the building. Seen from across the river or from the wharf, the tower is the first thing that catches your eye.
The building was begun by the Bureau of Public Works in the American colonial period and completed in
. Planning started in

, and it is said that an initial appropriation of ₱200,000 was followed by another ₱33,000 in 1917. The final plans were completed by Ralph Harrington Doane, who became consulting architect in 1916, while William E. Parsons and George C. Fenhagen took part in the earlier stages. Tomas Mapua is sometimes credited with the design, but that is a mistake: he joined the Bureau of Public Works only in 1917, when the building was almost finished.

Among the American-era customs houses that survive in the Philippines, it was the second to be built, after Cebu's, and it is counted as the second largest, after Manila's. It is less ornate than the Manila Customs House, but its orderly neoclassical balance has its own appeal. A customs house was built here because Iloilo was a port that prospered on sugar and textile trade. After the port opened to international trade in 1855, the British vice-consul Nicholas Loney brought European machinery and crop loans to sugar farming, the wharf grew busy, and today's street carries his name.
The building is still a working government office. Customs and immigration offices remain inside, and after the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) rehabilitated it in

, the Museum of Philippine Maritime History opened on the ground floor in January 2023. Admission is free, and it makes a short, easy stop on a walk through Iloilo's old downtown. Rather than expecting a big attraction, think of it as a place to enjoy the building itself, the riverside atmosphere and the museum's maritime stories together.

blocks.title: Neoclassical facade with a central tower

children.text: This neoclassical building is balanced on both sides of its central tower. Its decoration is simpler than that of the Manila Customs House, which gives it a clean, tidy look. Try to find a spot along the riverside road where the whole building fits into one frame.
This NHCP museum on the ground floor is open
Tuesday to Sunday

, free of charge. You can see miniature boats, navigational tools, artifacts from the NHCP collections and ethnographic items lent by other museums. It is a good, easy introduction to the long history Filipinos have had with the sea.

blocks.title: Gallery A: Early communities to the Spanish period

children.text: The gallery on the right as you enter covers maritime history up to the end of the Spanish period. It runs from the archipelago and early communities, to the Philippine seas and early European explorers, to the Philippine seas in the 18th century. Follow the maps and models slowly and read as you go.

blocks.title: Gallery B: American period to the present

children.text: The gallery on the left covers the period from independence to new colonizers, the Philippine seas today and the fishing industry. Because the customs house itself dates from the American period, the layout connects naturally with the history of the building.

blocks.title: Muelle Loney Street and the Nicholas Loney statue

children.text: On the street in front of the building stands a statue of Nicholas Loney, known as the "Father of the Philippine Sugar Industry." Once you know why Iloilo was such a wealthy port, the building makes much more sense. Some guides also say old stone warehouses still stand along the riverside, which are worth a look. Whether individual buildings are open and in what condition, however, you will need to check locally.

blocks.title: Views of the Iloilo River and Sunburst Park

children.text: The building faces the Iloilo River and Sunburst Park. Around sunset the light spreads across the river and makes good photos. It is pleasant to continue along the riverside promenade from here and enjoy the atmosphere.

Because the NHCP rehabilitated the building, the exterior and the ground-floor exhibition space are fairly well kept. Please remember that the other floors are working offices, since this is still an active government building.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: The customs house and an old-town museum on foot

children.text: Walk from City Proper to the customs house and first take in the facade and central tower from outside. The museum opens at
, so right after opening is the quietest time.
Enter the maritime history museum on the ground floor (free). Gallery A on the right covers history up to the Spanish period and Gallery B on the left covers the present, which takes about
40 minutes to 1 hour
Step outside and walk along Muelle Loney Street past the Nicholas Loney statue and the riverside, taking photos.
Head toward J.M. Basa Street and visit the NHCP's Museum of Philippine Economic History (Ynchausti building). It is reported to be open Tuesday to Sunday,
, and free, but check the latest information.
For lunch, try local food such as Iloilo's famous La Paz batchoy at a restaurant in City Proper.
The museum is closed on Mondays, so on a Monday change the plan to focus on the building's exterior and a riverside walk.

items.title: Full-day Iloilo history route
items.subtitle: From the customs house to Calle Real and a church

children.text: See the customs house and museum first.
Move to the Iloilo River Esplanade and walk through the modern riverside park.
After lunch, walk along Calle Real in the old town, where old buildings cluster.
Take a taxi or jeepney to Molo Church (about
3 km
away) and admire its Gothic-style exterior.
Return to the riverside and end the day watching the sunset scenery.
There are direct flights from Manila (NAIA) to Iloilo International Airport (ILO), and the flight takes a little over an hour. Airlines and schedules change by season, so check before you book.
The airport is in Cabatuan, about
from City Proper, and the trip usually takes
30–45 minutes
From the airport to the city, a taxi or Grab costs roughly ₱350–600, and a UV Express van to the SM City Iloilo area costs about ₱100–150. From there you need to transfer to a jeepney or taxi.
Fares vary with traffic and time of day, so confirm the fare before you ride.
From the center of City Proper the building is within walking distance, and the museum entrance is on the J.M. Basa Street side.
Jeepney routes 3, 5, 9, 10, 11, 18 and 25 are described as passing through City Proper. Routes and stops can change, so confirm them locally.
Grab or a taxi is convenient when you come from other areas such as SM City, Molo or Jaro.

items.title: By boat from Bacolod or Guimaras

children.text: The fast ferry from Bacolod to Iloilo takes 1 to 1.5 hours, and fares vary widely, from ₱250 to ₱800, depending on the operator and class.
The passenger terminal may not be right in front of this building but at a separate Iloilo fastcraft and RoRo terminal, so confirm the terminal location and then come by taxi.
Much of what you do here is outdoors on foot, so the dry season (roughly November to May) is more comfortable. December to February in particular is relatively cool and good for riverside walks.

During the June to November rainy and typhoon season, sudden showers are frequent and boat services can be disrupted. The museum is indoors, so it works well as a rainy-day alternative. The museum is closed on Mondays, so be sure to check the day of the week.

Most visitors stay in the old downtown of City Proper, near SM City, or around Iloilo Business Park. If you are only coming to see this building, a City Proper hotel is better for getting around on foot, while Iloilo Business Park is more convenient if you also want shopping and restaurants. Room rates change from season to season, so please check them directly.

Iloilo is known as a food city in the Philippines. Local dishes such as La Paz batchoy and piaya are easy to find in City Proper and nearby streets. There is no large restaurant strip right in front of the customs house, so after the museum we suggest walking toward J.M. Basa Street or Calle Real to eat.
The museum is open Tuesday to Sunday,
, so visiting before lunch is relaxed.
Many guides place the museum entrance on the J.M. Basa Street side. Check the signboards locally to find the main door.
For exterior photos, shoot from the river side so the tower and roof fit in together. The light is good around sunset.
Pair it with the NHCP's Museum of Philippine Economic History in City Proper and the National Museum Western Visayas for a one-day history tour.
We could not confirm the rules on photography inside the museum, so ask the staff.
Because it is a working government office, dress neatly and do not enter office areas.
When using Grab or a taxi, say the destination as "Iloilo Customs House" or "Aduana" and the driver will understand.
This building is still used by customs and immigration offices. Apart from the ground floor with the museum, the spaces are office areas, so do not go upstairs on your own.
Opening hours and closing days may change. The museum may be closed on Mondays and holidays, so check the latest notice.
Some past visitors mention climbing the tower to take photos, but access may now be restricted, so do not count on it.
The riverside and wharf area can be quiet late at night, so use a taxi or Grab after dark.
In the rainy season there can be sudden showers and flooding on some roads.
Ferry terminal locations may differ by operator, so be sure to confirm the terminal location before you buy a ticket.
A promenade built along the river, about
10 minutes
by taxi from the customs house. It is good for a walk at sunset.
Information on the whole city, including City Proper where the customs house stands. Combine food, churches and museums.
A church famous for its Gothic-style exterior, about
3 km
from the customs house. Go by taxi or jeepney.
One of Iloilo's best-known cathedrals, about
4 km
away. Its bell tower and plaza atmosphere are impressive.
Within walking distance are the Nicholas Loney statue, the Iloilo Provincial Capitol and the National Museum Western Visayas. Enjoy exploring on foot.
